blocks.text: Levita (in the Tishbi) says: “From אוז the pl. is אוזים, from אווזא the pl. is אווזות, more correctly אווזאות,” which, however, Buxdorf (Lex. p. 39) rightly disputes, since both the emphatic א and the א of the feminine ending are lost in the pl. The domestic goose differs from the wild one (§. 243) in that it has a longer bill (קועיה Rashi: ביק, Bec**), and in that the male has the penis and the testicles further below the diaphragm, whereas in the male of the wild goose they lie higher up. With this compare Aristotle (Thierg. 3, 1, 4); he says, in other words, that in the goose, soon after copulation, the testes, which lie below the diaphragm, [p. 191] become visible; apart from this time the testes (in the form of two acorns) lie further down; now, since the wild goose is smaller and slimmer, the testes will probably be visible on top at all times, which is what is meant in our Talmud passage.

The two species further differ in that the domestic goose has several eggs on the ovary at the same time, whereas the wild goose gets an egg on the ovary only once it has laid the previous one (B. Kama 55a). For these reasons of difference the two species may not be crossed with each other.
It should be noted that Sch. Aruch (Yoreh De'ah §. 297, 7) gives only that second, admittedly most essential, distinguishing criterion. —

The goose is a water bird and therefore, after the manner of these birds, has a very thin cerebral membrane (Chulin 56b). If one holds the goose's wings up, it still walks on, whereas the hen then draws its feet up as well and thus cannot walk. (Sabbat 128b; this lies in the difference of the muscular system of the two birds.) The flat side of the goose's foot is as broad as it is long (Bechoroth 45a). As a rule the goose returns to the coop in the evening (Beza 24a), yet it sometimes leaves the house and settles in gardens (Chulin 38b). The cackling of geese gave rise to the saying: He who sees a goose in a dream may hope for wisdom, for thus it is written (Spr. Sal. 1, 20): Wisdom cries aloud outside (Berachoth 57a); the goose also sometimes emits a whistling sound, which it produces through the nostrils with the bill closed; Rashi (Aboth 2, 10) calls this sound: שיפלור, siffler. Geese (the Jerusalem Talmud Ketuboth 26, d adds hens as well) cry out when someone suddenly passes by them (Ketuboth 27a); in another passage there (B. batra C. 8. H. 7) the expression is found: כרון אחון קקו פריפט “You cackle like geese.”

The exclamation “White geese!” expressed a rebuke against judges who were hoary and yet self-seeking; people said: “The white geese strip people of their cloaks” (Gittin 73a). With the same expression a rabbi paid women a not very delicate compliment: “He can,” he said, “remain unmoved at the sight of women, for they seem to him like white geese” (Berachoth 20a); from this passage we take merely the element of dazzling whiteness, such as the feathers of some geese possess.

[p. 192] The uses of this bird are manifold. Besides the eating of its flesh, the fat in the uppermost little wing joint (כנייל, probably כניכל, knuckle) also served against mouth rot (Joma 84a*). For external diseases of the mouth the mixture was applied with a bird's feather (Gittin 86a). The lung had special medicinal power. People used to say: “A goose costs one Sus, but the lung alone costs four Susin” (Chulin 49a); here, to be sure, the medicinally prepared goose lung is meant. The down feather (כלומא, Pluma, which, however, is more correctly called מלס, Molasse §. 76) was laid on the spot of the lung of a slaughtered animal that was thought to be injured, for the slightest draught of air passing through the injured membrane when the lung is inflated sets the feather in motion (ibid. 46b). Finally, geese were used for threshing (Sanhedrin 29b).
On the moulting of the goose cf. §. 246, note ***.

אוז בר (B. Kama 55a). One may not cross it with the domestic goose, since the two species differ in many respects. The female of the wild goose always has only one egg on the ovary, whereas the domestic one has many eggs on the ovary at the same time; in the male of the wild goose the testes lie higher up, in that of the domestic goose lower down, but in both below the diaphragm (see §. 242); finally, the wild goose has a shorter bill than the domestic one. Although קויה means neck both in quadrupeds (B. Kama ibid.) and in birds (Chulin 28a), Rashi nevertheless translates the word in our Talmud passage by ביק, Bec, bill, because in fact the bill of the wild goose is much shorter than that of the domestic goose, whereas the neck in both species is equally large in proportion to size. Cf. the appendix s.v. אוז הים.

בר אוזא (Beza 32b). The prefixed בר, בן, or בת does indeed designate the young of the animal (§. 1), yet בר אוזא does not mean “young goose” but, as it were, “little goose,” just as Latin Anas is related to Anser; cf. on this my contribution in the “Lien d’Israél” (2nd year, p. 364). In Jehuda ha-Lewi (in the Kusari ch. 3, §. 35) the duck is called אלברכיה, Arabic اَلْبَرْكِيَةُ [al-barkiyatu].

The duck has the habit of running to and fro with lowered head, rooting everywhere with its bill to seek food, and at the same time constantly looking about. From this arose the proverb: שפיל ואזיל בר אוזא ועיניה מטייפי “The duck stoops and walks on, and its eyes roam about,” by which a twofold thing was designated: first, a gossiping woman who sits at the distaff and meanwhile occasionally chatters and gossips about others (Megilla 14b), just as the duck searches while looking about, at the same time going forward.
